newsitem.title: UK: Tiny oilfield blamed for Neste's woes.
newsitem.headline: Tiny oilfield blamed for Neste's woes.

text.p: A tiny North Sea oilfield that failed to live up to its promise lies at the heart of a huge $100 million trading loss at Finnish oil company Neste Oy, industry sources said on Friday.

The sources, some of whom are familiar with Neste's trading position, said the losses were not due to "rogue" trading such as that which characterised recent trading scandals at London-based Barings and Japan's Sumitomo.
Badly-timed political pressure to privatise the Finnish company, forcing it to reduce exposure in the oil market, may have compounded the trading losses, they said.

The losses propelled Neste to a shock January-August loss before extraordinaries and tax of 26 million markka ($56.7 million), announced on Friday, and sparked the exit of many Neste traders including the head of its oil trading and supply division.
A month ago, Neste said it was tightening procedures and reporting in its crude trading unit to avoid future losses.

The company on Friday said the losses stemmed from the 1980s when it sold its stake in an oilfield, which it did not name, and simultaneously struck a long-term deal for the sale of crude oil produced from the field. It said Neste's loss was now limited and could even shrink because any further rise in cil prices would benefit the company.

A source familiar with Neste's trading strategy gave a few more details, saying trouble began when Neste overestimated the amount of oil to be produced at the North Sea field called Emerald in which it once owned a stake.

Neste hedged its production assuming a level of about 10,000 barrels per day when it only ever produced half that. Emerald stopped producing earlier this year after just four years of operations when it had tapped only eight percent of its reserves, analysts Wood Mackenzie say.
"(Neste) overhedged the field. It estimated 10,000 barrels per day but it actually got just 5,000," a source said.
Companies producing crude oil in the North Sea routinely hedge their production by selling forward derivatives to protect them against potential price falls.
This hedging has been particularly popular in the past two years given the volatile oil market trading conditions.

Neste sold its stake of Emerald when it began producing oil in 1992 but apparently only bought back part of its short (oversold) positions on crude derivatives, sources said. Ironically, for two years the short position did well, traders say. The average price of North Sea benchmark Brent crude oil fell from $18.15 in February 1992 to $13.65 in February 1994.
But then the market turned higher and in an effort to manage its short position Neste sold "range swaps" to Wall Street banks active in oil derivatives.

Range swaps set a floor and ceiling for the price of benchmark Brent crude. Neste recieved a fixed premium from the banks when the deal was struck. But it had to pay the banks for every cent that Brent prices went outside the set range.
Typically $4 a barrel ranges were set such as $14 to $18 a barrel, $15 to $19 and $16 to $20, sources said.
Brent prices rose relentlessly higher from February 1994 and as each ceiling was reached, the pressure on Neste was to buy Brent to help them hedge payments to the banks.

This was happening at a time when the company was trying to reduce speculative oil market exposure ahead of privatisation. This pressure hampered Neste traders' ability to offset the losses by playing the futures market, traders said.
"The blind drive to privatisation was the final blow," one source said.
Industry analysts saw Neste's problem as a one-off, unlikely to have a long-term impact on the company or on the global multi-billion dollar oil derivatives business.
They pointed to bigger losses by Sumitomo in copper and Metallgesellschaft AG in oil that did not drive most players from the derivatives markets.

"When one looks to hedge, one should have a very clear sense of what kind of (financial) exposure you have," said Charles Adams, vice president of Morgan Stanley in New York recently. --London newsroom 542 4984
